title: The envelope
learned: A gate says when a note starts and ends; the envelope turns it into a shape
Attack, decay and release are times; sustain is a level held while the gate is on
Envelope into the amplifier's CV: the volume follows the shape of every note

steps.why: A real note changes over time: a piano hits hard and fades, a violin swells in. The shape of that change is the envelope. It needs a gate: a voltage that is on while a key is held. Here a clock plays the part of the finger: it sends a gate on every eighth note (you will meet clocks in the Rhythm lessons).
steps.do: You hear the filtered sawtooth from the last lesson, droning. In the rack there is also a clock (JX-CLK), an envelope (JX-ENV) and a scope. Press Next.

steps.why: The envelope starts its shape when its GATE input goes on.
steps.do: Drag a cable from X2 of the clock to GATE of the envelope.
steps.after: The envelope now runs on every eighth note, but you hear no change: its output ENV goes nowhere yet.

steps.why: The envelope should control the volume, so it goes to the level input of the amplifier.
steps.do: Drag a cable from ENV of the envelope to CV 1 of the amplifier.
steps.after: Notes! With a cable in CV 1 the amplifier is closed at 0 V and fully open at 10 V. The envelope goes from 0 to 10 V and back for every gate, so every note gets the same volume shape.

steps.why: To see the shape, send the envelope to the scope as well.
steps.do: Hold Ctrl and drag a second cable from ENV of the envelope to IN 1 of the scope.
steps.after: The green trace shows each note: a rise (attack), a fall (decay) to a level (sustain) that holds while the gate is on, and a fade (release) after it ends. If the shape is too fast or too slow to see, turn TIME / DIV of the scope.

steps.why: Attack and release decide how a note begins and ends.
steps.do: Press F1 and turn ATTACK of the envelope up and down, then RELEASE. Watch the scope and listen.
steps.after: A short attack makes a hard start, a long one fades the note in. A long release lets the note ring after the gate is off; the notes start to overlap and blur.

steps.why: Sustain is different: it is not a time but a level.
steps.do: Turn SUSTAIN all the way down, then turn DECAY.
steps.after: With sustain at zero the note dies away even while the gate is on, and DECAY sets how fast: a plucked or struck sound. A high sustain gives an organ-like sound that stays loud as long as the key is held.
steps.try: Flip MODE to AD: the envelope ignores how long the gate lasts and only rises and falls. LOOP makes it repeat by itself without any gate.

steps.do: Gate says when, the envelope says how. Press Next to finish.
